title: Travel Agent: the 12-Part Framework Worked Through
subtitle: Critique a five-agent travel assistant whose draft pipeline does not match how agents run, then redraw it cache-first with agent-owned tools and a synthesiser.
author: By Sourav Banerjee

practice_prompts.label: The five faults in the draft
practice_prompts.hint: Name each fault, where it sits in the draft and why it wastes or blocks work.

practice_prompts.label: Redraw and trace the corrected design
practice_prompts.hint: Trace one request through a cache hit and a miss: which agents run, which tools each calls, where Policy overrides Booking.

practice_prompts.label: Defend the trade-offs
practice_prompts.hint: Shared or per-agent retrieval, regional or global stores, and when a new agent earns its cost.

practice_prompts.label: Gaps and customer questions
practice_prompts.hint: Cacheable queries, agent timeouts, ownership of shared services, and the targets only the customer can set.

rubric: I placed rate limiting inside the API gateway and explained why a dead-end box is a policy, not a component.
I put the semantic cache before the supervisor spawns anything and wrote the synthesised reply back to it.
I let only the needed agents start, and made retrieval a tool each agent calls in its own loop (Search and Recommendation yes, Booking and Policy rarely).
I drew the LLM, MCP registry, external APIs and vector DBs as a shared backend each agent calls on demand, so Booking reaches Flight and Payment during its own work.
I named a synthesiser that settles conflicts, with Policy overriding Booking, and stated what it does when an agent fails or times out.
I defended shared versus per-agent retrieval and named drawing RAG as a peer of the agents as the real mistake.
I weighed regional against global stores without claiming regional stores equal GDPR compliance.
I left the cache hit-rate and p95 latency targets open until the customer supplies residency rules and traffic mix.

editorial_review.evidence: Compared all 29 captured sections (7 intro, 14 Worked Example, 8 12-Part Framework) item by item with the previous casebook, which was 21 KB against 31 KB of source text and had compressed the five faults into two paragraphs. Restored: a heading per fault (rate limiter, cache, retrieval, shared turn, synthesiser) with the source's reasoning, the 'short-circuiting' term, the ten-step ordered data flow, the architecture legend, the audience, objectives and assumptions, 'Microservices' in the maintainability row, each reference's supporting claim, cache hit rate and reply write-back in the takeaways, and the interview lens as five questions with reveals. Fixed: the level paragraph that claimed Staff answers own cacheability (the table says no such thing); the checkpoint answer that invented principle names (now says the principles document is not in the case and only short-circuiting is named); the reconstruction figure, which omitted the dead-end rate limiter. The two source tracks repeat components, NFRs, trade-offs and the airport table, so each is merged into one table or deep dive with the framework-only wording kept. The brief now expands AMER/EMEA/APJ, defines agent loop, supervisor, synthesiser and semantic cache, and traces an illustrative Frankfurt-to-Singapore request through both drawings, since the source has no sample query. Cacheability rules, timeout handling, the agent-admission rule and the MCP authorisation caveat are labelled as this casebook's reasoning; follow-up drills are labelled as added. Source inconsistencies resolved in text (2026-11-16): worked example says 'a careful review found five' faults while the 12-Part Framework says an architecture review found four and an independent blueprint added the fifth → the framework's more specific account is used throughout (brief: 'two independent reviews found five'; walk-original states review-four plus blueprint-fifth as fact), since it is compatible with the worked example's total of five and names who found the synthesiser fault. November 20 complete maintained-baseline review: Complete maintained casebook: brief and Frankfurt trace, ten walkthrough steps, three figures, the ten-step data flow, non-functional table, all deep dives (components, cache, retrieval, regions, multi-agent, MCP, airport, sources), every checkpoint, lens and follow-up answer, calibration and Quick review.
